read.sections.0.heading.source: Spending now and saving for later
read.sections.0.heading.back: Spend now, and save for later

read.sections.0.text.source: Some choices affect only today, but others affect what we can do later. To spend means to use money or another resource to get something now, such as food or a bus ride. Spending is not bad, because everyone needs some things now. To save means to keep some money or resources for later. Saving is hard when there is not much, but small amounts can add up over time. Sami puts a few coins in a tin at home until he has enough for a notebook. In some communities, neighbours save together in a group. Each person puts a small amount into the group every week, and each week one person takes it all.
read.sections.0.text.back: Some choices affect only today, but some affect what we can do later. Spending is using money or other resources to get something now, such as food or a bus ride. Spending isn't bad, because everyone needs some things now. Saving is keeping some money or resources to use later. Saving is hard when you don't have much, but small amounts of money can build up over time. For example, Sami puts a few coins in a tin at home until he has enough to buy a notebook. In some communities, neighbours save together as a group. Each person puts a small amount of money into the group every week, and each week one person takes all the money.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Some choices are for today. Some are for later. To spend is to use money or things now. Everyone needs to spend on some things, like food. To save is to keep some money or things for later. Many small amounts make a bigger amount. Sami puts a few coins in a tin. Soon he can buy a notebook. Some neighbours save as a group. Each person puts in a little every week. Each week, one person takes it all.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Some choices are about today. Some are about days ahead. Spending is using money or things now. Everyone has to spend on some things, such as food. Saving is keeping some money or things to use later. Small amounts of money, many times, can add up to a big amount. For example, Sami puts a few coins in a tin. Soon he can buy a notebook. Some groups of neighbours save together. Each person puts in a little money every week. Each week, one person takes all the money.

read.sections.1.text.source: A budget is a plan for how to use money or time. It helps you compare what you have with what you need and want. Budgets are not only for money. Mei makes a time budget for her evenings. She plans time to help with dinner, to rest and to read English for 15 minutes. Budgeting is really about choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. If Mei reads for 15 minutes, she has 15 fewer minutes for games on the shared phone. This is a trade-off: giving up one thing to get another. A careful budget helps you see your trade-offs before you choose.
read.sections.1.text.back: A budget is a plan for how to use money or time. A budget helps you compare what you have with your needs and wants. A budget isn't only about money. For example, Mei makes a time budget for her evening. She plans time to help cook dinner, rest and read English for 15 minutes. Budgeting is really about choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. If Mei reads for 15 minutes, she has 15 fewer minutes to play games on the shared phone. This is a trade-off: giving up one thing to get another. A carefully made budget helps you see trade-offs before you decide.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A budget is a plan for your money or time. It helps you see what you have and what you need. Mei makes a time budget for her evenings. She helps with dinner. She rests. She reads English for 15 minutes. So she has less time for games on the phone. That is a trade-off. You give up one thing to get another.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A budget is a plan for using your money or time. It helps you see what you have and what you need. Look at Mei. She makes a time budget for the evening. She helps cook dinner. She rests. She reads English for 15 minutes. So she has less time to play games on the phone. That is a trade-off. You give up one thing to get another.

read.sections.2.text.source: A goal is something you want to do or get, and you work towards it step by step. Nobody can control everything about the future, and plans can change when things around us change. That is why small, short goals are useful. They are goals you can work on now, such as learning 10 new English words a week, practising a skill or staying healthy. A strong plan is also flexible. Mei's Plan A is to read every evening. Her Plan B is to read at lunchtime if the evening gets busy. A flexible plan still works when life changes.
read.sections.2.text.back: A goal is something you want to do or get, and you reach it step by step. No one can control everything in the future, and plans can change when things around us change. This is why small, short-term goals are useful. They are goals you can start now, such as learning 10 new English words a week, practising one skill or keeping healthy. A good plan also needs to be flexible. Mei's Plan A is reading every evening. Her Plan B is reading at lunch break if the evening is busy. A flexible plan still works even when life changes.
read.sections.2.text.note: Plan A / Plan B kept as แผน A / แผน B, as Thai speakers say. 'flexible' is ยืดหยุ่น (glossary).

read.sections.2.simpler.source: A goal is something you want to do or get. You work towards it step by step. No one can control the future. Plans can change. So small goals help. You can work on them now. For example, you can learn 10 new words a week. A strong plan is flexible. Mei's Plan A is to read in the evening. If the evening is busy, she reads at lunch. That is her Plan B.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: A goal is something you want to do or get. You reach it step by step. No one can control the future. Plans can change. So small goals help. You can start them right now, such as learning 10 new words a week. A good plan must be flexible. Mei's Plan A is reading in the evening. If the evening is busy, she will read at lunch break. That is her Plan B.

write.example.source: The goal is for Sami to buy a notebook and two pens for English class. Each week, he will put half of any coins he gets into a tin at home. He will save these coins and give up some sweets. The trade-off is fewer sweets now, but a notebook later. If things change, Plan B is to ask the learning centre for a spare notebook he can use until he has saved enough.

If something changes, Plan B is to borrow a spare notebook from the learning centre until he has saved enough.

watch.summary.source: This short video for younger learners explains spending and saving. People use money to get the things they need and want. But no one can have everything they want. This is called scarcity, so people must make choices. People usually get what they need before what they want. For example, the speaker needs a healthy lunch but wants a cupcake. So lunch comes first. Then the speaker checks if there is money left for the cupcake. When you spend, you get something now. But it may be small, and you may have little money left. When you save, you have to wait, and that can be hard. But later you can get something that costs more. There is no one right answer. Think about the good and bad sides of each choice.
watch.summary.back: This short video was made for younger learners and explains spending and saving. People use money to get needs and wants, but no one can get everything they want. This is called scarcity, so people have to choose. People often buy needs before wants. For example, the speaker needs to eat a healthy lunch but wants a cupcake. So lunch comes first, and then the speaker sees whether there is money left for a cupcake. When you spend, you get something now, but it may be something small and you may have little money left. When you save, you have to wait, which can be hard, but later you get something more expensive. There is no single right answer. Think about the pros and cons of each choice.

watch.keyPoints.2.back: There is no single right answer; think about the pros and cons of each choice.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: The lesson avoids pay, bank accounts, loans and long career plans on purpose. Keep discussion to small, short goals that learners can control. Do not ask learners where they will live in future or about their household's money. If a learner finds talk about the future upsetting, return to the small goals in the lesson and do not press.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson deliberately doesn't talk about wages, bank accounts, loans or long-term career plans. Keep the discussion on small, short-term goals learners can control. Don't ask learners where they will live in the future or about their family's money. If a learner feels uncomfortable talking about the future, go back to the small goals in the lesson, and don't push.
sensitiveNotes.0.note: 'do not press' is อย่าเร่งเร้า. Check the tone suits adults working with displaced youth.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: The video opens by saying that many people earn money by working, and its examples are a cupcake, an ice cream and a toy. Preview it; the written summary leaves out the part about working.
sensitiveNotes.1.back: The start of the video says many people earn money by working, and the video's examples are cupcakes, ice cream and toys. Watch the video first. The written summary doesn't mention the part about working.

educatorNotes.0.source: The Friday savings group is a rotating savings group. These are found in many parts of the world under local names; the FAO source lists, for example, susu (Ghana), arisan (Indonesia), ekub (Ethiopia) and tontines (West Africa). A partner can use a local name. Present it as something adults organise, based on trust, not as advice for learners to join one.
educatorNotes.0.back: The Friday savings group is a rotating savings group, found in many places around the world under local names. The FAO source gives examples such as susu (Ghana), arisan (Indonesia), ekub (Ethiopia) and tontine (West Africa). Partner organisations can use a local name. Present it as something adults organise based on trust, not as advice for learners to join.
educatorNotes.0.note: Local names (susu, arisan, ekub, tontine) kept in Latin letters as in the source. The Thai name (แชร์) was not added, since the brief says to add no Thai example; the partner note already invites a local name.

educatorNotes.1.source: Sami's tin, Mei's time budget and Rosa's water filter can be swapped for local examples, such as saving phone credit or data, or planning study time around chores and classes.
educatorNotes.1.back: Sami's tin, Mei's time budget and Rosa's water filter can be changed to local examples, such as saving money for phone calls or internet, or planning study time around chores and class periods.
